questions.q: What are the two main narrative threads in "Lost Spring" and where does each take place?
questions.a: The two threads are Saheb's story (a ragpicker in Seemapuri, Delhi) and Mukesh's story (a bangle-maker's son in Firozabad, Uttar Pradesh). A wrong answer — such as naming three threads or placing both in the same city — reveals the student hasn't grasped the deliberate dual-structure that anchors the entire text.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the author's role as a first-person narrator shapes the narrative structure of "Lost Spring."
questions.a: The author acts as a witness and bridge: she enters each world, records conversations, and reflects on what she sees, making the structure feel like a journalistic investigation rather than a detached report. Her presence ("I ask", "I see", "I wonder") creates narrative cohesion across the two separate locations. A wrong answer that treats her as an invisible third-person narrator misses how her voice stitches the fragments together and signals the text's persuasive purpose.

questions.q: The text moves from Saheb finding a rupee in garbage to him carrying a steel canister at a tea-stall. What structural purpose does this shift serve?
questions.a: It marks a narrative turning point: from childhood autonomy (ragpicking, where the bag is "his" and he is "his own master") to bonded labour (tea-stall, where the canister belongs to the owner and he loses his carefree look). This micro-arc within Saheb's story mirrors the larger structural movement from relative freedom to systemic entrapment. A student who only notes "he changed jobs" misses the structural symbolism of the bag vs. canister.

questions.q: Compare the narrative endings of Saheb's and Mukesh's stories. What does the structural asymmetry suggest about the author's message?
questions.a: Saheb's story ends in resignation (working at a tea-stall, "no longer his own master"), while Mukesh's ends with a fragile, geographically limited dream ("I will walk" to a garage, but not fly a plane). The asymmetry — one child's agency extinguished, the other's dream narrowly surviving — structures the text's argument: systemic forces crush most, but resistance, however small, exists. A student who says "both have sad endings" flattens the deliberate structural contrast Jung builds.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of Jung's choice to interweave the Udipi temple anecdote (the priest's son who prayed for shoes) within Saheb's narrative. Does it strengthen or disrupt the narrative structure?
questions.a: It strengthens by providing a temporal and thematic counterpoint: the anecdote jumps thirty years forward to show a "success story" (the priest's son now wears shoes), which ironically highlights how little has changed for ragpickers. The embedded narrative acts as a structural foil — past vs. present, prayer vs. reality, individual mobility vs. collective stagnation. A student who calls it a "digressions" fails to see how non-linear inserts serve the text's argumentative structure.

questions.q: Write a 50-word narrative fragment from the perspective of a third child in Firozabad who *does* join a cooperative, using Jung's structural techniques: sensory detail, dialogue, and a final line that echoes the "web of poverty" metaphor.
questions.a: A strong answer will include: (1) concrete sensory detail (smell of solder, heat of furnace), (2) a line of dialogue showing collective action ("We met at the temple, twenty of us"), (3) a closing metaphor linking to the text's central image ("The web trembled but did not break"). A weak answer will be generic, lack Jung's observational tone, or miss the metaphorical echo.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Plot and Narrative Structure in "Lost Spring" refers to the author Anees Jung's deliberate organization of two parallel real-life narratives — Saheb the ragpicker in Seemapuri and Mukesh the bangle-maker's son in Firozabad — into a cohesive non-fiction account that moves from intimate observation to systemic critique, using first-person narration, dialogue, contrast, and thematic ______ rather than a conventional linear plot.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're ______ a documentary that follows two children in different cities but cuts between them to show how their stories mirror each other.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) map the dual narrative arcs of Saheb and Mukesh, identifying how each progresses from introduction to conflict to unresolved tension, and (2) explain how the author's structural choices — alternating portraits, embedded anecdotes, shifting tone — serve the theme of stolen childhood and systemic poverty.
